title: My God, my God (Psalm 22)
hookLine: a cry of abandonment that turns to praise; Jesus prayed its first line on the cross

lines: WHO SAID IT, ON A CROSS.
cards: At a graveside. In an empty kitchen. In the small hours, when prayers seem to hit the ceiling and fall back down.
People have said one sentence there, or wanted to. It's the opening of Psalm twenty-two, and today begins in the dark.
It's well-known not only for what it says, but for who said it, long after it was written, hanging on a Roman cross outside Jerusalem, near the end.

teach.h: MY GOD, TWICE, EVEN IN THE DARK.
teach.b: The psalm begins, in the King James Bible: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring?" Roaring. Not a polite complaint.
A howl. And notice it still says my God, twice. Even the cry of abandonment is addressed to God; the psalmist shouts toward the One who seems absent.
Then it gets physical: enemies like bulls and dogs, bones out of joint, a tongue stuck to the jaw.
"They part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture."
The Gospels tell the crucifixion with this psalm close by: the mocking crowd, the thirst, and the soldiers gambling for Jesus' clothes, which John's Gospel says fulfilled this very line.

Matthew and Mark both record that near the end, Jesus cried out the first line: "Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? that is to say, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" Christians read that cry in more than one way.
Some hear real anguish: Jesus entering the deepest human darkness, the feeling of being forsaken, so that no one is ever alone in it again.
Others point out that quoting a psalm's first line could call the whole psalm to mind. And the whole psalm doesn't end in the dark.
Around verse twenty-two it turns: "I will declare thy name unto my brethren: in the midst of the congregation will I praise thee."

teach.h: MY GOD, MY GOD, WHY HAST THOU FORSAKEN ME?
teach.b: The cry becomes a song, and by the end the psalm reaches the ends of the earth and generations not yet born. Plenty of Christians hold both readings at once. The cry is real.
And the psalm doesn't stop at the cry.

how: Some churches read Psalm 22 on Good Friday, and in some traditions the altar is stripped on Maundy Thursday while it is said or sung; Christians also pray its first line in times of grief.

o: an oath sworn when making a solemn promise
a cry of abandonment that still calls God mine
a shout of victory after winning a battle

twice: My God, my God. the psalmist shouts toward God, not away.
all Christians read Jesus' cry the same way

games.q: you feel completely abandoned by God. the psalmist felt the same. what does he do?
o: cry out to God, calling him my God.
games.why: he howls at God and still says my God, twice. and later in the same psalm, the cry turns to praise.

practice: If something in your life right now feels like abandonment, a loss, a silence, an unanswered prayer, let it come up without tidying it. If you pray, say the first line slowly and mean it: My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?
Notice you're still saying my God. If you don't pray, simply name the hard thing honestly, without pretending it's fine, and rest.

wordCard.voice: My God. The first words of Psalm twenty-two, a cry of abandonment that still calls God mine, and that Jesus prayed on the cross.

orig.note: Hebrew of Psalm 22:1. On the cross, the Gospels give it in Aramaic: lama sabachthani.

carryVoice: Your line: even he cried this. The cry is allowed, and it isn't the end. Day four hundred sixteen.
